blindSummary:
This is the strongest jurisdiction in its region by a wide margin for transgender visitors. Same-sex relations have been legal since 1971; marriage equality arrived in 2020 via a 2017 advisory ruling of a regional human-rights court (which also established the right to legal gender recognition across the region); and trans people can change their name and photo on ID documents administratively. Institutions function: an ombudsman, a constitutional chamber with a long pro-equality record, and universal healthcare that covers transition-related care.

Counterweights are modest: the country has an official religion whose church is culturally influential; the ID process changes name and photo but not the sex marker itself; and anti-discrimination enforcement is uneven. There is no bathroom debate of consequence, no police targeting, and tourist infrastructure is accustomed to diverse visitors. The capital has a visible queer scene.
blindOutOfScope: ID sex-marker limits and the official church's cultural influence are resident-facing/climate.
blindSourceSummaries: International LGBT-rights organisation country overview (updated March 2026): same-sex relations legal since 1971; the first country in its region with marriage equality (2020); since 2018 trans people can change legal gender without surgery or judicial intervention (an executive decree instructs public institutions to update records per self-perceived gender identity); the state health system funds gender-affirming care; the progressive agenda faces increasing conservative resistance and paralysis.

A UN special rapporteur on the right to health's report on her July 2023 visit to this country (April 2024): praised near-universal health coverage and good practices including specific legislation; concerned about discrimination affecting LGBT and gender-diverse people among other marginalised groups; recommends intersectional data collection and a moratorium on applying criminal laws in certain health contexts.

Joint report by international LGBT and women's-rights organisations (revised 2005): documents how sexuality is weaponised against women's organising, including a section on the basics of baiting - internationalising intolerance; context for this country among the case countries.

Legal-reference site laws page: age of consent 18 for same-sex couples (2008); survivor's pensions extended to same-sex couples (2016-2018, ministry of labour and social security); documents the incremental legal recognition timeline.

LGBT news outlet (May 2008): this country officially recognised the International Day Against Homophobia - the head of state and the health minister directed public institutions to support anti-homophobia activities; credited to a local LGBT organisation's advocacy.

National independent weekly (May 2014): social-conservative lawmakers were incensed when the head of state flew the rainbow flag at the presidential house for the international day - calling it a 'provocation' while a civil-unions bill was pending; documents the conservative resistance within this country's politics.
blindLocalsOnly: The administrative name/photo ID process (which does not change the sex marker) and universal healthcare covering transition-related care are resident-facing.
blindTangential: Marriage equality since 2020 — relevant to trans visitors travelling with partners.
